questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Place the child on the side, maintain a safe airway position, assess breathing and responsiveness, and continue close observation while the child recovers from the seizure.","B":"Give oral fluids immediately to replace losses from fever because swallowing can be assumed to be safe once generalized shaking has stopped and the child is no longer convulsing.","C":"Restrain the child's arms and legs during the postictal period because limiting movement prevents another seizure while the temperature is being rechecked and treated.","D":"Insert an object between the teeth after the seizure to protect the tongue because oral injury remains the main immediate danger once the convulsive activity has ended."}}
questions.rationale: After a generalized febrile seizure, immediate priorities are safety, airway and breathing assessment, and recovery positioning. A drowsy child should not be given oral fluids until fully alert and able to swallow safely. Restraining the child or placing objects in the mouth does not prevent seizure injury and can cause harm.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Febrile Seizures in Children / Seizure First Aid
questions.source_detail: AAP guidance emphasizes protecting the child from injury, maintaining the airway, and seeking evaluation after a febrile seizure; objects should not be placed in the mouth.

questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A barky cough that occurs mainly when the child cries, with no stridor at rest and normal color, is the finding that most strongly indicates impending upper-airway failure.","B":"Mild hoarseness with a low-grade fever and comfortable breathing is the finding that most strongly indicates severe croup requiring emergency airway intervention.","C":"Intermittent cough with normal air movement and no retractions is the finding that most strongly indicates progressive airway obstruction from severe croup.","D":"Stridor at rest with retractions or increasing fatigue indicates more severe upper-airway obstruction and requires urgent evaluation rather than routine home observation."}}
questions.rationale: AAP guidance identifies a barky cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor as typical of croup. Stridor at rest, retractions, increasing work of breathing, fatigue, cyanosis, or inability to speak/drink indicate more severe upper-airway obstruction and require urgent evaluation.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Pediatrics — Croup in Young Children
questions.source_detail: AAP notes that stridor at rest and increasing breathing effort are signs of more severe croup that need medical evaluation.

questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Pain that remains localized to the epigastrium and improves after eating is most consistent with appendiceal inflammation progressing toward perforation and generalized peritonitis.","B":"Pain that migrated from the periumbilical area to the right lower quadrant with focal tenderness is compatible with acute appendicitis and warrants prompt surgical evaluation.","C":"Burning dysuria with suprapubic discomfort and urinary frequency is the classic progression of appendicitis because urinary symptoms usually precede right-lower-quadrant tenderness.","D":"Diffuse cramping relieved by defecation with no fever or focal tenderness is the pattern most concerning for acute appendicitis requiring immediate operative evaluation."}}
questions.rationale: Acute appendicitis classically begins with vague or periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed. Localized right-lower-quadrant or McBurney-point tenderness, often with nausea or fever, warrants prompt evaluation because delayed diagnosis increases the risk of perforation and abscess.
questions.source_detail: Current clinical review describes periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant and localized McBurney-point tenderness as classic appendicitis findings.

questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings are most consistent with uncomplicated postoperative pain because hypotension after cardiac surgery commonly causes jugular venous distention without impaired filling.","B":"The findings suggest isolated left-sided heart failure because muffled heart sounds and rising venous pressure are expected when pulmonary congestion is the only problem.","C":"The combination of hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds raises concern for cardiac tamponade and requires immediate escalation for evaluation.","D":"The findings are expected after cardiac surgery and can be observed until the next routine assessment because tamponade typically presents with hypertension and flat neck veins."}}
questions.rationale: Cardiac tamponade occurs when pericardial pressure impairs cardiac filling and output. Hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds are concerning classic findings; after cardiac surgery, new hemodynamic deterioration requires immediate escalation because tamponade can rapidly become life-threatening.
questions.source_name: American Heart Association — Pericarditis Complications: Cardiac Tamponade
questions.source_detail: AHA describes tamponade as pressure from pericardial fluid that impairs filling and pumping and can cause a dangerous fall in blood pressure.
